title: Podcast with Johannes Pollanen, Co-founder of EeroQ and a Professor of Physics at Michigan State University - Quantum Computing Report
gist: In a podcast transcript, EeroQ co-founder Johannes Pollanen argues that CMOS semiconductor manufacturing is the only proven path to scaling quantum computers, and pitches electrons floating on superfluid helium atop foundry chips, with a 10,000-qubit (still NISQ) chip targeted in a couple of years. He is skeptical of IBM-style networked dilution refrigerators and says the key open problem is building a big system.

insights.claim: EeroQ's core thesis is that a quantum computer can only be scaled via CMOS semiconductor manufacturing, because that is the only scalable computing architecture humanity has invented; the alternative is inventing an equivalent, which he judges harder than solving the remaining quantum and error-correction problems.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Frames the bet: manufacturability, not qubit physics, is the moat, favoring foundry-compatible modalities.
insights.quote: in all of human history, we’ve never figured out how to make lots of anything on the computational side, except for transistors in silicon
insights.locator: Transistors and silicon

insights.claim: EeroQ designs chips that are manufactured by a commercial semiconductor foundry using the same standard processes as iPhone and laptop chips, then adds a superfluid helium film and electrons on top; the company says it is now at the stage of integrating its in-house single-qubit devices with foundry-made chips.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Foundry reliance lowers capex and could shorten scaling timelines if integration works.
insights.locator: Is that thing behind you using helium-3?

insights.claim: The quantum field has no 'transistor' yet: modalities (superconducting, trapped ion, neutral atom, silicon spin, photonic, electrons on helium) are competing, and he compares them to punch cards versus vacuum tubes, where only the scalable technology wins.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: No modality winner is established, so portfolio exposure across modalities is rational.
insights.quote: we haven’t yet found, you know, the transistor of quantum computers
insights.locator: The modalities of quantum computing

insights.claim: He argues none of the modalities is perfect and that all can be successful to some level; the hard part is finding one that combines the benefits of all.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Suggests a multi-winner market rather than winner-take-all in the near term.
insights.locator: Quality or quantity of qubits

insights.claim: EeroQ qubits are single electrons held about 10 nanometers above a thin film of superfluid helium-4 on a semiconductor chip, in vacuum, using electron spin as the qubit and requiring no lasers for readout (on-chip circuits are used instead).
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Core technical differentiation from ion and neutral-atom systems that need laser control.
insights.locator: The modalities of quantum computing

insights.claim: Helium never freezes because it is very light (large quantum zero-point motion) and chemically inert with filled electron shells, so it stays a perpetual superfluid; at these temperatures everything else is frozen, so the electron sees no magnetic or charge noise from impurities.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Explains the claimed qubit cleanliness advantage over solid-state platforms.
insights.locator: You’ll need liquid helium

insights.claim: Superfluid helium has the highest thermal conductivity of any known substance near absolute zero, which EeroQ says helps extract heat from chips and addresses power-dissipation problems at scale.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Heat removal is a scaling constraint for dense chips; this is claimed as a natural advantage.
insights.locator: How do you cool quantum systems?

insights.claim: The electrons-on-helium qubit idea was proposed in the 1990s and first trapping experiments date to the late 1960s and early 1970s at Bell Labs, but the community was siloed from quantum computing until academics began applying superconducting-qubit readout techniques.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: The platform is old physics with new tooling, but is later to qubit maturity than peers.
insights.locator: How do you cool quantum systems?

insights.claim: EeroQ's chip architectures are designed so electrons can be shuttled to run error-correcting codes, like ions and neutral atoms, which gives connectivity that fixed-position superconducting qubits lack.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Qubit mobility is the architectural hook for next-generation error correction.
insights.locator: How do you do a computation on a qubit?

insights.claim: The Wonder Lake chip, about 3 by 5 mm, was designed to hold roughly 2500 electrons, but since each qubit uses two electrons (singlet-triplet), that gives about half as many qubits, and the chip is a demonstrator for error-correction choreography rather than a thousand-qubit device.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Corrects naive electron-equals-qubit counting; actual qubit count is far lower.
insights.locator: Is that thing behind you using helium-3?

insights.claim: EeroQ's goal is a 10,000-qubit chip within the next couple of years, connectable to the cloud or sold on-premise, and he concedes even that would be an NISQ machine, not the full-scale machine needed for the biggest problems.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: A near-term, falsifiable milestone; also an admission that 10,000 qubits is not fault-tolerant scale.
insights.locator: How do you make more qubits?

insights.claim: The long-term target is millions to tens of millions of electrons on a chip not much bigger than the current few-millimeter device, which he says is roughly a doubling of chip size.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Density per footprint is the claimed route to a single-fridge fault-tolerant machine.
insights.locator: Is that thing behind you using helium-3?

insights.claim: EeroQ built its first charge qubits on helium in about 18 months and published first coupling to an electron-on-helium charge qubit in Nature Physics earlier this year; the next steps are two-electron spin qubits, measured fidelities and two-qubit gates.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Marks real progress but shows spin qubits and gate fidelities are still unproven.
insights.locator: How do you make more qubits?

insights.claim: Pollanen admits EeroQ is 'a little earlier than most' on the quantum part (qubit quality) but 'way ahead' on scaling, and he doubts many peers have ideas for building large-scale systems.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Explicit trade: weaker qubit maturity for a claimed scalability lead; execution risk sits on qubit fidelity.
insights.locator: How do you cool quantum systems?

insights.claim: EeroQ claims it works faster than academia by using fab, design, theory and measurement teams in parallel, cracking in 18 months a readout idea that had been around for more than 10 years.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Supports the venture-spinout model for deep-tech speed.
insights.locator: How do you make more qubits?

insights.claim: Current 10,000-qubit chips will be relatively slow, similar to neutral atoms or ions, but EeroQ says it has trade-secret methods for much faster gates and is building first prototypes; he lists quality, quantity and speed as all required.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Gate speed is an undisclosed, unverified differentiator.
insights.locator: Faster quantum computers

insights.claim: He says the biggest unanswered challenge in quantum computing is how to build a big system, since toy-scale machines already exist across modalities and the open question is a machine big enough to be useful.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Industry value now hinges on scale-up engineering rather than proof of principle.
insights.quote: How to build a big system.
insights.locator: Faster quantum computers

insights.claim: He is skeptical of superconducting-qubit scaling: each qubit carries a millimeter-scale length, qubits differ from one another, and IBM's route is, in his words, brute force, networking many dilution refrigerators together.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Interconnected-fridge architectures carry engineering risk that could delay IBM-type roadmaps.
insights.quote: quite brute force to build big systems with lots of dilution refrigerators network together
insights.locator: Can IBM make a useful quantum computer?

insights.claim: He nonetheless declines to say IBM will miss its goals, calling himself an internal optimist who expects all modalities to keep succeeding for a while, with much work still left for every approach.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: His critique is relative, not a bearish call on incumbents.
insights.locator: Can IBM make a useful quantum computer?

insights.claim: EeroQ aims to put as many densely packed qubits as possible into one dilution refrigerator, perhaps two or three, rather than building thousands or tens of thousands of fridges.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Fridge count drives cost and cryogenic supply demand, so density is a competitive lever.
insights.locator: Can IBM make a useful quantum computer?

insights.claim: Quantum algorithms are not hardware-agnostic: surface code assumes nearest-neighbor connectivity, while newer quantum LDPC codes require long-range connections, achievable either by swap chains or by physically moving qubits.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Hardware that can move qubits (ions, atoms, EeroQ) fits LDPC codes better, which changes which platforms scale efficiently.
insights.locator: How do you do a computation on a qubit?

insights.claim: Connectivity is a major differentiator, and ions, neutral atoms and EeroQ 'really shine' because qubits can be moved around.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Competitive landscape for error-correction efficiency favors mobile-qubit modalities.
insights.locator: How do you do a computation on a qubit?

insights.claim: He is most excited by chemical simulation and drug discovery, and says the biggest applications need millions or tens of millions of physical qubits and many logical qubits, not 100 logical qubits; cybersecurity via Shor's algorithm is real but secondary.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Value case is pharma/chemistry at large scale; near-term revenue depends on small-molecule simulation access via cloud.
insights.locator: Reverse engineering quantum computing

insights.claim: Small-scale molecular simulation on cloud-connected quantum computers already happens (for example via Amazon Braket), which he says few predicted five to ten years ago, and he says progress has been faster than he expected.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Cloud access is an existing channel for monetization and learning.
insights.locator: Quantum computing at a wedding

insights.claim: Each dilution refrigerator uses about 20 liters of helium-3 gas, which is recirculated and not lost; helium-3 is extremely rare (about one part per million of the roughly one part per million helium in air), so fridge builds depend on finding new sources.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: Helium-3 supply is a hardware-scaling bottleneck that favors designs needing fewer fridges.
insights.locator: Is that thing behind you using helium-3?

insights.claim: EeroQ's chips use common helium-4, not helium-3; helium-3 is needed only for the cooling system.
insights.speaker: Johannes Pollanen
insights.so_what: EeroQ's chip material has no rare-isotope dependency, though its fridges still do.
insights.locator: Is that thing behind you using helium-3?
